method: Before = worktree of bfba4da (861fd62 + download_hour, the code the prediction was made against); after = this branch. Run alternately before, after, before, after, 7 runs each, same session, same cached inputs (input_sha256 in each record). Records: automation/runs/m0-s5/bench/.
keep_rule: From the plan (docs/MILESTONES.md, M0-S5 Accept-when): a parser optimisation is kept only if it meets its committed prediction and the contract's output hashes are identical; additionally the after/before IQRs must not overlap on every reference hour.

P1.evidence: fingerprints identical on both hours; apply minus parse ~1.11 s before vs ~1.14 s after (within 10%)

P2.evidence: 1.835 s pooled median vs <= 1.35 s predicted; 21% faster vs >= 28% predicted
P2.why: orjson parses these lines ~1.5x faster than json.loads, not the 2.5x assumed, and the 19-digit guard adds ~0.13 s per hour; the eager decode the argument expected to remove was a small share

P3.evidence: heavy hour gained 18.1% vs 21.1% on the typical hour

predictions.decision: REVERTED. The change was faster (IQRs disjoint, hashes identical) but missed its committed prediction P2, and the Accept-when keeps a parser optimisation only if it meets that prediction. An IQR-only keep rule was briefly written after seeing the numbers; it was withdrawn as moving the bar. events.parse is json.loads again; the measurements seed a new refine issue with a re-derived prediction (target M1-S5).

attempt_1.what: the same change with a regex guard, re.search(rb'\d{19}') per line
attempt_1.result: slower than before: 2.91/3.26 s vs 2.09/2.17 s (typical), 6.90/7.95 s vs 4.06/4.13 s (heavy); the regex scan alone cost 1.40 s and 4.93 s per hour, more than json.loads
attempt_1.fix: bytes.translate digits to '0' then a substring search: 0.13 s and 0.46 s, flagging exactly the same 294 and 921 lines

after_revert.uv_lock: package set identical to before orjson was added
